title: August and the Room
premise: Late-night radio host Paloma Quintana has spent three weeks taking calls from listeners who died the previous week — a phenomenon she alone hears, and one she keeps secret to protect her sanity and her sister's family, the Delgados, whose farmhouse she fled to after her breakdown. When her childhood imaginary friend, August, appears unchanged on their porch, Paloma realizes the calls are the house's way of counting its residents before it 'closes the doors' and keeps them. As the count climbs toward the number of living souls inside, Paloma must choose between the duty of silence that kept her alive and the love that demands she break it, rallying the Delgados — skeptical, grieving, and frightened — to escape before the final tally. The story ends with Paloma staying behind to finish the count herself, trading her place on the ledger for the family's freedom, only to discover August took her name off the list years ago and has been paying the debt ever since.
about_author: Xanthe Joubert is the pen name of a former overnight radio producer from the Karoo who swears the switchboard lit up twice after a caller's obituary ran. August and the Room is their second novel, written entirely between midnight and four a.m.

chapters.title: Dead Air, Warm Voices
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. On air at 1 a.m., Paloma takes a call from a regular listener, then learns the man died six days ago. She keeps her voice steady, logs the call, and counts the locks on her door twice. The beat is controlled dread — the reader learns the rules of her secret world before she admits them to herself.

chapters.title: The House That Keeps a Ledger
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. She arrives at the Delgado farmhouse where her sister-in-law Marisol, brother Tomás, and niece Ines take her in. Paloma notices the house has too many doors and one that's always cold; she counts eleven rooms and hears twelve breathing. Emotional beat: the fragile comfort of found family shadowed by wrongness.

chapters.title: August
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. On the porch at dusk sits August, her childhood imaginary friend, unchanged after thirty years — same corduroy overalls, same too-wide smile. He says, 'You kept the lights on. Good. The count likes lit houses.' Paloma's terror wars with a lifetime of longing for him. Beat: love and dread in the same face.

chapters.title: Ines Sees Him Too
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Nine-year-old Ines has been drawing a friend named August for weeks, though she's never met him. Her drawings show the house with every window filled with watching faces. She tells Paloma at bedtime. Beat: the horror becomes generational; the children were always the intended audience.

chapters.title: The Caller Who Knew My Name
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. A radio caller describes the farmhouse's kitchen, the cold door, Ines's drawings — then says, 'The count is at four. It was at five when you were a girl. You cost it one.' Paloma realizes her childhood escape left a debt. Beat: guilt reframes her survival as theft.

chapters.title: Marisol's Grief
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol, still mourning her mother's death last month, hears her mother's voice on the baby monitor. She doesn't tell Paloma; she starts leaving the porch light on. Beat: grief makes the family vulnerable — the house feeds on the bereaved, and Marisol is its easiest door.

chapters.title: Rules of the Count
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. August, over cold coffee he never drinks, explains: the house counts souls at each new moon; when the count matches the living, it closes. He was made to be her friend so she'd stay. He's been stalling the count for thirty years. Beat: August's love revealed as a long, quiet sabotage of his own purpose.

chapters.title: Tomás Doesn't Believe
chapters.summary: Tomás's POV. Tomás finds Paloma's notebooks of dead callers and nearly throws her out, terrified for Ines. But the cold door is warm on his side and ice on hers, and the hallway is one step longer at night. Beat: the skeptic breaks — not through proof, but through his body's refusal to lie.

chapters.title: The Eleventh Room
chapters.summary: Paloma and Ines's alternating POV. They find a twelfth room that only appears in Ines's drawings: wallpaper of names, thousands, and fresh space at the bottom. Ines touches it and a name appears — her own, half-formed. Beat: the stakes become a child's erasure; Paloma's protective love ignites into purpose.

chapters.title: Static and Confession
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. On air, Paloma breaks format and confesses everything, begging dead listeners for how to break a count. The switchboard lights with a hundred voices at once, all repeating: 'Uninvite what you invited.' She understands: August must be sent away, and it will feel like losing him again. Beat: duty versus love made explicit.

chapters.title: The New Moon Rises
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. The count reaches eight. Lights flicker in sequence, doors open and shut in order, and the family gathers in the kitchen without discussing why. Marisol's mother's voice thanks them for leaving the light on. Beat: the household unifies in fear — found family forged in the dark.

chapters.title: What August Was For
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Paloma remembers: lonely, unloved at seven, she invented August and 'invited' him to live in her grandmother's house — this house. He never left. Every imaginary friend invited here becomes a door the house can count through. Beat: Paloma's childhood solace was the infection's origin; her love is literally the mechanism.

chapters.title: Uninviting
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. At the threshold, Paloma formally uninvites August. He goes — smiling, saying 'You always kept the lights on' — and the count drops to seven. But the house, cheated, begins taking rooms instead: the kitchen vanishes overnight, then the bathroom. Beat: victory that costs them the house itself; the siege begins.

chapters.title: Rooms Going Dark
chapters.summary: Tomás and Marisol's POV. The family wakes to fewer rooms each morning, the house folding inward like a closing hand. They plan escape by car, but the driveway now leads back to the porch. Tomás admits he believes — and apologizes to Paloma. Beat: despair, then the first true solidarity.

chapters.title: The Voice on the Switchboard
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Paloma rigs the farmhouse radio to the station's frequency. The dead callers, all former residents who were counted, coach her: the count can be satisfied by a name freely given, but the house must accept it before moonset. Beat: hope with a terrible price tag — someone must stay.

chapters.title: Marisol's Bargain
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol secretly offers herself — she wants to see her mother again. Paloma catches her at the cold door and stops her; the sisters-in-law fight, then weep, then plan together. Beat: love against duty inverted — Marisol's duty to the dead vs. Paloma's love for the living.

chapters.title: Ines Draws the Way Out
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Ines, the house's chosen audience, realizes she can draw rooms that no longer exist — and briefly walk through them. She draws a hallway to the road. It holds for ninety seconds at a time. Beat: the child becomes the family's architect; hope becomes a practiced skill.

chapters.title: The Count Reaches Nine
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. The house accelerates, counting Ines's drawings as residents. Doors seal. The family runs drills through Ines's paper hallways as walls close in, moonset hours away. August's voice comes through the radio static: 'I'm still paying your debt. Don't waste it.' Beat: breathless escalation toward the climax.

chapters.title: Moonset
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The climax. Paloma gives her name to the count at the cold door — freely, fully, speaking her childhood invitation in reverse. The house accepts, the doors unlock, and the family flees down Ines's last drawing as the farmhouse folds shut behind them with Paloma inside. Beat: sacrifice as the answer to every theme at once.

chapters.title: The Room With Her Name
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, inside. Paloma wakes in the eleventh room, wallpapered with names, and finds hers already crossed out — in a child's handwriting, thirty years old. August kept her off the ledger all along; the count took her now only because she offered. Beat: devastating tenderness — her sacrifice was unnecessary, and entirely hers.

chapters.title: The Last Broadcast
chapters.summary: Paloma and August's POV. In the folded house, August shows her the truth: he can leave if someone stays willingly, and he has been waiting three decades for her to choose to stay so he could go free. Instead, they rewrite the wallpaper together — uninviting the house itself, name by name. Beat: love against duty resolved as shared rebellion.

chapters.title: Keeping the Lights On
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, epilogue. The Delgados find Paloma on the highway at dawn; the farmhouse is an empty lot that was never built on. Paloma returns to the radio, no longer taking calls from the dead — but every night at sign-off she says, 'Goodnight, August,' and somewhere, static breathes back. Beat: quiet, earned resolution — found family intact, survival's price acknowledged, love outlasting the count.
